utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, sir. The affirmation you made still applies. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojanovski.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning. Yesterday, we reviewed a financial award that you received in June of 2001, as well as a pistol which you received in October 2002. And I suggested to you that pursuant to the Law on Internal Affairs, the minister has the final authority to decide on awards, and I misspoke at that time. The minister's authority actually comes from the collective agreement of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could please show the witness what is Exhibit P382, and if the witness could be given a copy of the first Defence binder that Ms. Residovic used. Actually, Ms. Usher, there's one more. If you show me that binder again. Yes. This is the Prosecution's binder. There is -- what I'm referring to is the first Defence binder. You should have number one as well. It was used yesterday. It was number one. If not, I can give the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if my colleague wants to use other documents, we could give our binder to the witness so that the Prosecutor can use his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance, Mr. Stojanovski, if you turn to tab 14 in that binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which tab was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was tab 14, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 14. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- in the first Defence binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is -- if you see the first page, Mr. Stojanovski, you can see that this is the collective agreement of the Ministry of Interior. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn the pages until you reach Article 85, please. Do you see Article 85 now, Mr. Stojanovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment. I will give the witness my copy; and, unfortunately, I also have -- I also have that page missing in the original Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could be of assistance, Your Honours, I believe that the Prosecutor has this exhibit noted in a wrong tab. The witness would be able to find this document, but the sequence of documents is not proper, I believe. But I'm sure he would be able to find this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The witness can see the Article on e-court, if we can just stop focussing on the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stojanovski, you'll see that Article 85 says that: "The employee with special engagements and quality in execution of the work and assignments, who will contribute significantly to the process of realisation of the ministry's function, will be given a reward in the amount of one salary." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't think the interpreters heard you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you look at the next paragraph in that Article, and it's on the next page in the English version, the next paragraph says: "The proposal in item 1 of this Article is submitted by the manager of the organisational unit, and the decision for reward is brought by the minister or an employee authorised by him." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So can we agree, then, that the final decision regarding who receives an award from the Ministry of Interior is made either by the minister or a person authorised by him?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I believe we went through this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you asked to see the particular law, and so that's why I'm showing it to you now. Yesterday, at the end of my questioning, I asked you whether, in 2001, the OVRs of the Ministry of the Interior were outside the normal chain of command of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and you responded: "They're obligated by the Book of Rules, if this is what you have in mind." And I'm not sure that you actually answered my question, and so let me rephrase it, hopefully more simply: Do the OVRs fall within the chain of command of the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OVRs, the departments of internal affairs, are organisational units within the Ministry of Interior, if we look at the ministry as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So can we take that response as a "yes"?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you take into account the entire structure of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned earlier in your testimony - this was in response to a question from Ms. Residovic, at page 9102 of the transcript - that within SVR Skopje, 2001, there were five OVRs, and you said: "Within the territory of the OVR," of a particular OVR, "only the members of the OVR can carry out ministry matters." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The internal affairs matters are carried out at the territory of the OVR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. But you said last week, at page 9102, that: "Within the territory of the OVR, only the members of the OVR can carry out Ministry of Internal Affairs matters." Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is within the division of work in the Ministry of Interior. However, if we speak about the police competencies, then, in the cases when the police officer is found within the territory of another OVR as well, they have the right to undertake the necessary actions should he be, for instance, present when an event is developing or should he need to offer assistance to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And following that logic, suppose, in 2001, for example, someone with a higher level of responsibility arrived in a particular OVR, let's suppose the director of the bureau for public security, and it would be possible, wouldn't it, for the director of public security to address affairs of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in the territory of a particular OVR? Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that the director can be present within the territory of another -- of a particular OVR, but it does not change the competences that they have pursuant to the organisational structure and the systemization of the MOI.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the director of public security, for example, the director of the bureau of public security, as an authorised official of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, would be able to carry out his competences within the territory of a particular OVR. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't fully agree with this assertion. As I stated, within the Ministry of Interior, there are rule books on systemization of jobs, organisational structure. The Law on Internal Affairs sets for the competences, in general; however, the division or distribution of tasks is regulated through the rule book on systemization.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, suppose, for example, the director of public security was driving through, for example, OVR Cair one day and witnessed a crime. Certainly, the director of public security, as an authorised official of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, could take certain responsible steps at that time to try to report that crime or even resolve it. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As any other citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, as any other citizen or also as a member of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, he would have a duty, wouldn't he, to take certain steps?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To provide further clarification, shed light on this issue, it would be good to see the Law on Internal Affairs which also covers the rule book and the systemization. So any officer in the ministry, in addition to the general competences they have, they also have direct tasks and competences assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is Exhibit P86. It's the Law on Internal Affairs, and it should be tab 2 in the binder that the witness has in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovski, is there anything in the Law on Internal Affairs that would prevent the director of the bureau of public security from carrying out his duties within the territory of an OVR?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you said, nothing from within the remitt of his duties prevents him from that, his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. How about the minister? How about the minister himself or herself? Anything in the Law on Internal Affairs that would prevent a minister from carrying out some of his duties or her duties within the territory of an OVR?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no such provisions, so his competences can be performed, regardless of where he is located at the time, as long as it's within the territory of the Republic of Macedonia. However, I'm not sure, but I think that one has to take into consideration what are his competences and tasks within the ministry. So when we're speaking about his specific competences and tasks, there are no obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I interrupt, Mr. Saxon. Why do you limit his competences to when he is within the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. You're right. He, as a minister, could carry out official trips where some cooperation agreements are concluded, so he is performing his tasks then as well, if I managed to clarify. I was referring specifically to the Republic of Macedonia, but within the competences of the minister fall also competences in the area of international cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was thinking more simply. If the minister were in another country and a problem arose in his ministry, would not it be possible for the minister, having been informed of the problem, to make a decision and give a direction, even though he was then in another country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe you've got the Law on Internal Affairs in front of you, Mr. Stojanovski. Can you turn to the Macedonian version, please. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you take a look at Article 1, which begins: "Internal affairs, in the sense of this law, are the activities which concern the following," and then we see a rather long list of topics, beginning with protection of life; personal safety and property of citizens; prevention of criminal offences; solving criminal offences and apprehension of perpetrators of criminal offences and handing them over to proper authorities; protection of human and citizens' freedoms and rights as guaranteed by the constitute, et cetera. These are the competences of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, therefore, these are also the competences that would fall within the remit of the minister's work. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To clarify this a bit further, in every organisation, you have distribution of tasks. You can't expect every officer in the organisation to perform any and every task. So, although I am not a lawyer, it might be advisable to have a look at Article 24 of this law. I think that this Article, if we look at it together in conjunction with the systemization rule book, would resolve some of those aspects that we're discussing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where do you see within Article 24 a suggestion of limited competences of the minister?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your previous questions well, they are based on the competences, if I understood you well. The Article 24 defines which are the officers who have competences, authorisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. But, of course, the minister is really the highest officer, if you will, of the Ministry of Interior, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it? Highest ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, the person at the very top level of the Ministry of Internal Affairs is the minister, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you take a look at Article 1, please, of the Law on Internal Affairs, doesn't Article 1 then describe all the different areas that are within the responsibility of the minister as the highest-ranking official of the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is fine. However, if I succeeded in following your logic and drawing a parallel, if you have a Minister of Health, does it mean that the minister should perform surgeries, if, for instance, he is found at a hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If have you a Minister of Health, Mr. Stojanovski, that Minister of Health would have to be concerned about the quality and quantity of surgeries performed in hospitals in Macedonia, wouldn't he or she?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same logic applies to the Minister of the Interior. He is has the political responsibility for the quality of performance of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the Minister of the Interior would give instructions, then, about the performance of those competences to his staff, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it is the duty of the professional staff, services in the ministry to monitor the work and to propose directions aiming towards improving the quality of work; while the minister, as far as I understand it, has the duty to take care of all organisational aspects, to provide functioning, operation of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if the minister disagrees with a proposal, are you suggesting that the minister simply remains silent?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that he would be silent. However, I believe that through the independent bodies, through the bodies within the ministry, he would have communication and would resolve all the issues that he believes to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And those issues would fall within the list of affairs that are listed in Article 1 of the Law on Internal Affairs, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Stojanovski, during your direct examination, you described the relationship between the work of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the work of the public prosecutor. You explained - this is at page 9093 to 9094 of the transcript - you explained that if the Ministry of Internal Affairs receives information that a crime might have occurred, then the ministry has the duty to check out the facts and provide a minimum of relevant facts and information that might corroborate the suggestion that a crime occurred. Do you recall that? Do you recall explaining that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, so, it's important, then, at least when members of the Ministry of Interior first receive information that a crime might have occurred, that those colleagues, on their own initiative, investigate and establish - or try to establish - whether or not a crime has been committed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If you could turn to what is the third tab in that binder in front of you, Mr. Stojanovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, this will be Exhibit P88, and it's the Code of Criminal Procedure of Macedonia. If turn to Article 140, please, which is on page 32 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have Article 140 in front of you, Mr. Stojanovski?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Article 140 provides: "The state agencies and institutions which perform public authorisation are obliged to report crimes which are prosecuted ex officio of which they are informed or of which they learn about in a different way." So this particular Article would effectively codify what we discussed just a moment ago, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not completely sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to Article 142 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The first paragraph of Article 142 says that: "If there is a ground for suspicion that the crime is committed which is to be prosecuted ex officio, the Ministry of Internal Affairs is obliged to take over necessary measures to find the criminal, for the criminal or the collaborator not to hide or," I think the word should be "abscond," "for traces of the crime and objects which may serve as evidence to be found and obtained," et cetera. Wouldn't that paragraph effectively codify what we mentioned a moment ago, that if they're informed that a crime may have occurred, members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, on their own initiative, should do some investigation and establish whether the crime actually did occur?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could understand it in that way, apart from the use of the notion "investigation," because the investigation falls under the competences of the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll try to use another term then. Members of the internal affairs are obliged to take measures to see if a crime might have been committed. I won't use the word "investigation." Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And if you can turn to tab 8 in the binder in front of you, Mr. Stojanovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P96. It's the Book of Rules on the work of the Ministry of Interior, and if you could turn to Article 103, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have Article 103 now in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Article 103 says that: "When grounds exist for suspecting that a crime which is prosecuted in the line of duty has been committed, the authorised officials take the necessary measures to find the perpetrator or the accomplice, discover and secure evidence of the crime, and then collect evidence." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this would be then consistent with the Article 142 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you then take a look at Article 104 which has three paragraphs, the third paragraph says: "The existence of grounds for suspicion regarding a committed crime is confirmed through confirmation of direct evidence or by circumstantial evidence." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only quote that it's necessary to know relevant facts and data on the basis of which it can -- a serious presumption can be made that a criminal act was committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you have a provision at the end of Article 104 that refers to confirming grounds of suspicion via direct evidence or circumstantial evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, just as an example, if an authorised official of the Ministry of Internal Affairs saw a person who appeared to have been beaten, for example, that authorised official should then carry out his responsibilities with respect to Articles 103 and 104. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "duty," if you could explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, discover and secure evidence of a possible crime; find the perpetrator of the crime, if possible; speak to the person who appears to have been victim -- to be the victim and ask what happened to he or she. That would all be within the remitt of Article 103 and Article 104. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's a matter of translation again, but I understood that the authorised person encounters a person with visible injuries that measures have to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Measures have to be taken to evaluate whether that person was a victim of a crime, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important to know whether the person is reporting that he or she was a victim. Injuries could have incurred due to various other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Suppose the person is unconscious. Would you still have a duty, under Articles 103 and 104 to try to verify what happened to that person, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will respond with a concrete example. In the area of Cair, an authorised person found a person of Albanian ethnicity unconscious. This person was taken to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, you haven't answered my question. My question was simple. Suppose an authorised official of the Ministry of Internal Affairs sees a person lying on the street unconscious with signs that perhaps that person had suffered a beating, bruises, cuts, et cetera. Wouldn't the authorised official, under the Book of Rules on the work of the Ministry of Interior, Articles 103 and 104, have a duty to take measures to see whether that person was the victim of a crime?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above all, there is the duty to secure medical assistance and then to speak with that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, suppose that person is unconscious, wouldn't the duty still exist under Articles 103 and 104 of the Book of Rules and under Article 142 of the Code of Criminal Procedure?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. You explained that -- and these measures that the authorised official of the ministry should take, at least the authorised official has the responsibility to take those measures at least prior to the commencement of a formal investigation by a public prosecutor or an investigative judge, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorised official should do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But you also explained to my learned colleague, Ms. Residovic, that if the authorised officials of the Ministry of Internal Affairs don't find any relevant facts, then the case is archived or, as you put it, put on stand-by. That's right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if we don't find such information or data.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in those situations, you explained that the members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs do not have the obligation to inform the public prosecutor. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is no report of a crime, or we have not established in the course of our work facts or understanding that a crime has been committed, then no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please turn to Article 167 of the Book of Rules on the work of the Ministry of Interior, please, the same document that we've been looking at. Do you have Article 167 in front of you, please?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Article 167 says: "If on the basis of the collected information in other measures an actions taken for its confirmation and documentation, it is asserted that grounds for suspicion that a crime exists, which is prosecuted in the line of duty, the authorised official composes a criminal report which is delivered to the competent" and in English it says "publicity defender," that should be "public prosecutor." Then it says: "It should be submitted along with the criminal report, objects, sketches, photographs, supplemental reports," et cetera. Do you see that, Mr. Stojanovski?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you take a look please then at Article 168, it says: "The ministry informs the public prosecutor even when, on the basis of the information collected, there is no basis for submission of a criminal report." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So what you told us last week, that the Ministry of Internal Affairs has no obligation to report to the public prosecutor about the so-called stand-by cases, was not correct, was it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say so --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because these are different situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Authorised officials act or undertake measures for uncovering crimes but also act at the request of the public prosecutor. If, in this case, authorised officials acted or checked information at the request of the public prosecutor, then they're obliged to inform the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, but suppose the authorised officials are dealing with a crime ex officio, don't they still have the obligation to inform the public prosecutor about their activities and the fact that there appears to be no basis to suspect that a crime occurred?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they have no obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where does it say that in Article 168 or within this Book of Rules?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not tell you the exact Article, but I'm telling you on the basis of practice, established practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you --

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we act on our own, we undertake measures on the basis of which we expect to come to facts and knowledge whether a crime, an act has been committed or not; and depending on the outcome, we react on the basis on the outcome. If we work independently, we're not duty-bound to inform the public prosecutor. If we had acted at the request of the public prosecutor, then we are obliged to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we take a look again, please, at Article 167, Mr. Stojanovski, because in the third line, it specifically refers to crimes prosecuted in the line of duty; that is, crimes ex officio; I believe is the Latin term. That is a situation where no request has been submitted by a public prosecutor or investigative judge, at least not yet, and the Article 168 says that: "The public prosecutor must be informed when there is no basis for submission of a criminal report." So, at least as the rules are written, what you told us last week was not correct, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the rules, such an impression could be gained, but my 25 years of experience tell me to maintain my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Because, as you put it a moment ago, sometimes the practice of members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs may differ to a degree from what is written in black and white in the rules or laws. Right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're leading me into areas of legal regulations, and I said several times that I'm not an expert in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you're avoiding my question, Mr. Stojanovski. I'm not asking you about legal regulations. I'm asking you about practice, because you have, in the last couple of moments, volunteered that you, in your 25 years of practice, know that, in practice, certain activities might occur or not in a way that is different, for example, from what is written in the Book of Rules on the work of the Ministry of Interior. So if you could, please answer my question: The practice of members, the activities of members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, may differ, to a degree, from what is written in black and white in the rules or in the laws. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practical work is based on the rules and instructions for work in the Ministry of Interior and, above all, on the basis of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You still haven't asked my question. I'll ask it one more time. Sometimes, the practice of members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs may differ, to a degree, from what is written in black and white in the rules or laws. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree, because my interpretation is different than the one which you have presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it's true, isn't it that, the laws and the rules and regulations of the Ministry of Internal Affairs can't possibly address every possible situation or activity that a police officer, or members of the ministry, might have to address. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not heard of the existence of ideal laws or ideal rule books.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So we can take that response as a "yes"?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could understand this as it is not possible to have the law to foresee every -- every situation and to offer all possible solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that principle is particularly true, isn't it, in a period like spring/summer of 2001, when, as you described, the security situation in Macedonia was extremely complex?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the security situation was extremely complex, and I also said that my colleagues carried out their legal obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there were times, weren't there, when in order for your colleagues to carry out their obligations, sometimes they had to be creative or improvise and be flexible to ensure that those obligations were carried out. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Creativity is an important factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And that concept of creativity, that's not mentioned anywhere in this Book of Rules, is it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misinterpret me. Creativity is a quality which is required of all employees regardless of where they may be employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And creativity and flexibility is particularly important in crisis situations, in emergency situations, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is important, just as it is important for a person to be able to cope with stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, sometimes, when persons are under severe stress, they might carry out their duties in a way that would differ from the way they would act during peacetime, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such situations cannot be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to turn your mind, please, to another topic, and that is the demonstrations that occurred in the city of Skopje after the withdrawal of the NLA forces from the village of Aracinovo. In response to some questions from my colleague, at pages 9117 of the transcript, you described how, on the night of 25/26th June, 2001, you were present in front of the Macedonian parliament with your co-workers from the Ministry of Internal Affairs. You described how the demonstrators included civilians, reserve police officers, active police officers, members of the army who were upset about the events relate to the Aracinovo. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Minister Boskoski was present there?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Minister Boskoski was present, but we succeeded in protecting him because part of the forces that were engaged in front of the parliament had to be redirected towards the Albanian part for the protection of members of Albanian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask the witness to repeat the answer whether he said "succeeded" or "not succeeded."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stojanovski. The interpreters missed a portion of your last response and asked whether you could repeat your last response where you mentioned that you and your colleagues succeeded, or did not succeed, in protecting Minister Boskoski. That was not clear to the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not succeed in protecting him, nor did we succeed in protecting the parliament, because, at that moment, we had to act to protect the Albanian population, which we set out as a priority. When we weighed the protection of the parliament and the protection of the population, we decided part of the forces engaged to be redirected for the protection of the Albanian population and a smaller part did not -- this remaining smaller part did not succeed because they were few in number to fully respond to their duties and tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Risto Galevski, the head of the crime police, he was also present that night, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Galevski was not the head of the crime police. He was the head of the police unit. He was present and he held a speech, in a way, to try to calm down the people who were demonstrating and he succeeded in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And thank you for correcting me. You're absolutely right. I misspoke. Because at that time, it was Mr. Petrovski who was head of the crime police, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You need to speak into the microphone, sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably. My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you did not succeed in protecting Minister Boskoski. What happened to Minister Boskoski that night?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vehicles from his escort were destroyed, demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that the crowd of demonstrators that night was pretty angry.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I explained that they were dissatisfied by what we were duty-bound to do, that we facilitated members of the NLA to leave the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you explained a moment ago, you said "We decided that part of the ministry forces that were present near the parliament building would be re-directed for the protection of the Albanian population." Who made that decision? Where did that decision come from?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I was there on-site, and Mr. Bliznakovski and I believe Mr. Efremov; that is to say, SVR Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the police reservists who you saw in the crowd that night, can you estimate approximately how many police reservists were there in the crowd?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the crowd amounted to some 4 to 5.000 people, and I would only speculate about the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But you observed that a portion of that large crowd was made up of police reservists?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were these individuals wearing reserve police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were wearing police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were some of these police reservists carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did some of these police reservists fire their weapons into the air?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that some shots were heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Help us understand, please: How did you know that these individuals were police reservists?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's a simply question. You said that, and you've said it twice now, that part of the crowd of demonstrators that night was made up of police reservists, and you said that they were wearing police reserve uniforms and some of them were carrying weapons. My question is: How did you know that these individuals were police reservists?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received information from the heads of the OVRs that part of their reserve police officers refused to take the orders and started towards the parliament building. So, on the basis of that information, we surmised that those were reservists, if that is what you are thinking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did it help your evaluation process the fact that these individuals were wearing police reservists uniforms and carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not able to identify them. It might have been that some of them were not reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But you believed that they were reservists, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that I received from the head of the OVRs, departments for internal affairs, we believed that those were reservists. However, I will repeat: We did not succeed in establishing their identity. We did not manage to ask them for their IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So, just to summarize, you heard that these individuals were reservists and they were dressed in the uniforms of police reservists, and some of them were carrying fire-arms. So you --

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- believed that they were police reservists, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We surmised that those were police reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, in the summer of 2001, in a de facto sense at least, if you saw persons wearing reserve police uniforms and carrying fire-arms, you treated them like police reservists, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be certain, you need to ask them to show you their IDs or they need to show you their IDs if they are to undertake some activities. Every police reservists employed or activated by the Ministry of Interior needed to possess an ID, police ID. And until you established that a person had such ID, you could not be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then, why were you sure that these persons in the crowd on the night of the 25th of June in front of the parliament building were reserve police officers?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated that it was our surmise that those were police reserve reservists. I did not say that I was sure about that. I stated that we received information from the heads of the departments for internal affairs that part of the reserve forces has left the positions and started towards the parliament building. Whether, in all those people in front of the parliament, the entire crowd assisted of police reservists, I could not state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness, Your Honour, answered precisely what my objection was directed at. He said that at some point he wasn't sure whether those were, indeed, police reservists. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I delayed your objection because there was, at that point, a critical question to be answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand fully, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Saxon, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that to be certain whether someone was a police reservist, you would need them to show you their identification. Well, isn't it true that only in midsummer of 2001 that Minister Boskoski issued instructions for identification cards to be issued to reservists?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You need to know that the reserve police officers are carrying out their duties only in the presence of an active police officer. That is one aspect. The other aspect is the one that you mentioned. It is true that, at one point in time, a change was made to the rule books that regulated the issuance -- or rather, established the format, the mode of issuing of IDs for the reserve police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier, during that complex time in 2001, how stretched the resources of the Ministry of Interior were. Are you suggesting that all the members of the reserve -- of the police reserves quickly received a police reserve identity card?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about things outside of my competence. I believe that my colleagues, who were working on that, had a maximum of seriousness in the perform of their tasks and they performed it well. I can't speculate and I wouldn't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned a moment ago that the reserve police officers carry out their duties only in the presence of an active police officer. So another factor, if I can use a mathematical term in this equation, of determining whether someone is or might be a reserve police officer is whether they are in the company of an active member of the Ministry of Interior. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you explain why not?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since that was the practice, that was applied autonomously or independently by the heads of the departments for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you told us a minute ago you need to know that the reserve police officers are carrying out their duties only in the presence of an active police officer. That's what you told us just a minute ago. So why are you now telling us that this was actually just an autonomous or independent practice by the heads of the OVRs?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is like this: In the area governing the performance of tasks and working duties, whenever we had an opportunity, the active police officers were carrying out their tasks supported by reserve police officers. So, when it was necessary to establish a patrol, then, considering what we said previously that the resources were scarce, the practice was that the patrol head would be an active police officer, while the remaining members would be reserve police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, however, they also have all rights and obligations, but that doesn't mean that it has to be taken or considered as a guideline on the basis of which we would identify someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, all right, I think I understand your answer, but let me go back, then, to my last question. If you saw persons dressed in reserve police uniforms carrying weapons in the company of an active police officer, that would be another indication that these persons were actually reservists, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This would be indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- although, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovski, during your direct examination, you described many protests in front of the assembly of Macedonia by citizens who were not satisfied with the measures taken by the Ministry of Internal Affairs to suppress terrorists, or at least that's what I read in the transcript. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Wasn't it the army's job to fight the NLA?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were reviewing the Law on Internal Affairs a moment ago, and you read there the competences of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do we take your response as a "yes" or a "no," Mr. Stojanovski?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a task for both the army and the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why was it necessary for the members of the Ministry of Interior to get involved in fighting the NLA back in 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are taking me to a part that I'm not really competent to explain or speak about. There is a so-called national plan for defence in the Republic of Macedonia. In the Republic of Macedonia, there is a council for national security. I can't comment their work, nor their decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovski, maybe if I can simplify this. Was the security situation in Macedonia in 2001 so serious and so complex that the men, women, and resources of both of Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Internal Affairs were required to combat the NLA? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can provide to the witness the second binder provided by Ms. Residovic last week, and if we could show him what is tab 37 in that binder. Your Honours, this would be Exhibit 1D126.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovski, this is an information dated the 9th of August, 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the subject is: "Individuals who violated the public law and order and committed robberies on the 8th of August, 2001." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph, it says: "Following operative measures and activities by the OVR Centar, in connection with the disturbances and public law and order violations, as well as damage to and looting of shops and other buildings, a total of 44 individuals, 21 of whom were minors, were arrested and detained in police stations, Centar and Bit Pazar." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says: "Interviews were conducted with the individuals, and it was determined that 30 of them participated in the looting of the damaged buildings. A large part of the stolen objects which were discovered on the perpetrators was seized and will be returned to the rightful owners." Then below that, there is a list of the individuals who were arrested. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You testified earlier that after these demonstrations in the summer of 2001, once the situation was calm, the police would take measures to find the perpetrators of crimes that were committed, vandalism, looting, et cetera. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the situation calmed down?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After these demonstrations ended or calmed down, then the police would take measures to try to find the perpetrators of the crimes that occurred during the demonstrations. Do you remember explaining that to us?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With respect to the individuals mentioned in this particular report from the 9th of August, do you know how the police identified the perpetrators who are described in this document?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: By direct observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So, if I understand you, that means that certain police officers witnessed these particular crimes and these particular individuals committing the crimes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although, they found the perpetrators when leaving the crime screen and carrying out the stolen property.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And as part of their duties, then, these police officers would then arrest the perpetrators of the crimes who they observed, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to what is page 2 in the English version, and it's the last page in the Macedonian version. At the bottom of page 2 in the English version, there's a paragraph beginning with the word, "furthermore," but it's on the last page of your version, Mr. Stojanovski. Do you see that paragraph? Do you see the word "furthermore"?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "Furthermore, interviews with the individuals pointed out that Aleksovski, Marjan, known as Zver, also stole from the shops, together with four other individuals (Brle, Cikoi, Marjan, and Igor), and that they are in possession of the items. They're being sought for arrest in order to return the stolen goods." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, during the summer of 2001, another method that the Macedonian police used to identify perpetrators of a crime was to speak with other perpetrators, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although, the notion identification might not be appropriate to learn about other persons, but the identification is something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, another method that the Macedonian police used to learn about other potential perpetrators of a crime was to speak with perpetrators of the crime, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Citizens, perpetrators, witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the hour. Would this be the appropriate time to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will take the break now and resume at 11.00, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovski, if you could turn to what is tab 39 in the binder in front of you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 1D129.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stojanovski, you'll see that this is an information from 25 July 2001, regarding the security situation in the city of Skopje and the wider region in the period from 1800 hours to 2400 hours on the 25th of July, 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it describes, for example, in the first paragraph: "Another protest rally in front of the parliament; citizens from the Tetovo region were joined by a larger group of citizens from Skopje. And, then, in the second paragraph, it talks about how at around 2100 hours a group of around 1500 persons visibly revolted, headed toward to the publishing and printing house, Nova Makedonija, and set fire to several vehicles. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, in the next paragraph, it says that the same group headed to the government of the Republic of Macedonia, the General Staff of the army, as well as the embassy of the United States, and some of the demonstrators threw rocks at the embassy, breaking several windows. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, then, in the next paragraph, it talks about, during the movements of this crowd of people, there were vehicles and facilities that were damaged. Have you been following me?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn to tab 141 in that -- excuse me, tab 41 in that binder, it is 1D127. Are you able to find tab 41?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher could assist Mr. Stojanovski; if not, I can give -- oh, he's got it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see, Mr. Stojanovski, this is another information of the Ministry of Internal Affairs from the SVR Skopje, and it's dated the 9th of August, 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the subject is: "A protest of citizens in Tetovo and Skopje during which several facilities were damaged in the centre of Skopje." In the first paragraph, it describes how on the 8th of August, 2001, at about 4.00 in the afternoon, in front of the parliament, two large groups of citizens arrived to express their revolt about the terrorist act which happened on the road Skopje-Tetovo, and in which ten soldiers lost their lives. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the paragraph ends, that eventually the crowd reached about 4.000 to 5.000 citizens. Now, just to clarify, this demonstration or protest, this took place after the attack on the convoy at the area known as Karpalak, is that right, the attack on an army convoy?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, in the second paragraph, we see how the demonstrators placed barriers in different locations. They damaged the entrance door of the building of the government of the Republic of Macedonia. And, in the third paragraph, they turned over waste collection containers. Then it says, in the fourth paragraph: "At around 2030 hour, around 20 citizens from the mass, from the crowd, knowing that several wounded terrorists are being treated at the general city hospital, entered the hall of the hospital wanting to reach by force the intensive care unit. However, they were prevented in doing so and, therefore, they left the hospital." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, then, in the next paragraph, it talks about that there was damage to stores and other business facilities, as well as theft, and a total of 46 persons were detained. Have you been following me?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, now, this particular protest took place in August, first part of August. Would it be fair to say that by August of 2001, particularly after the deaths of members of the Macedonian security forces, that acts of violence against civilian property, and suspected terrorists even, were becoming fairly predictable?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in continuity. It was normal. This was nothing that could not be expected. We were facing a situation like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So the answer to my question, then, would be: "Yes, such violent reactions by this time became predictable for the police." Right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was the practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, so, again, by that time, by August 2001, the police would want to take great care [Realtime transcript read in error "carry"], for example, after incidents where members of the security forces were killed, in order to try to avoid danger to civilians in such a volatile environment. Would that also be true?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could say that, in accordance with the available resources we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just for the record, I see on page 36 of the LiveNote, line 3, I see the phrase take great "carry," that should be take "care."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Moving on to a different topic, Mr. Stojanovski. During your direct examination, in response to a question from my learned colleague, Ms. Residovic, at page 9106 of the transcript, you said: "According to the Law on Internal Affairs, members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs at the republic level have no operative functions." And you said: "The same is true for the minister." And you said that: "In the Law on Internal Affairs, there is no mention of an obligation pertaining to operative tasks." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The minister does not have operative functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, again, could we please provide to the witness what would be binder number 1 provided by the Defence, and if we can turn to what is tab 2. It's Exhibit P86, the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you, Mr. Stojanovski, could please turn to the Macedonian version. Mr. Stojanovski, we've already earlier today we looked at Article 1, which describes the competencies of the ministry. Can you take a moment, please, where it says -- take a moment, if you will, look through the Law on Internal Affairs and tell us where does it say that the members of the Ministry of Interior at the republic level, or the minister, have no operative functions. Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 1 does not establish the competencies of the minister --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- while Article 24 regulates these issues, together with the systemization manual for working places at the ministry. Article 24, then, which I mentioned, should be looked at together with the manual for organisation and work of the ministry, and the rule book for systemization of workplaces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does it say anywhere in Article 24 that the minister or members of the ministry at the republic level have no operative functions?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we were to read the law in its entirety, not just Article 24, we could see that it lists the competencies of the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you take me to that Article in the law?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Which Article is that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say, for example, Article 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. In the English version, Article 75 says: "Within one month from the time when this law has come into effect, the minister will bring general acts for organisation and work and for systemization of the posts in the ministry." That's what Article 75 says, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the obligations of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does Article 75 tell us that the minister cannot play a role in operative matters?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not obligate him. There is a difference, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether the minister is obligated to do something. I'm asking you whether anything in this law or in Article 75, since you brought us to this Article, prohibits the minister from becoming involved in operative matters.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not prohibit, but this would be outside his authorisations and competencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law regulates the competencies of the minister --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn back to Article --

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because the minister cannot be considered as a police official, as a police officer. I don't believe anywhere in the world you will be find -- you will be able to find such a solution. This is not the case in Macedonia. The minister is a political figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The minister is also an authorised official, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. This is why I mentioned Article 24, which attempts to regulate this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And as one of the authorised officials, perhaps I should say as the highest authorised official in the ministry, the minister would have a lot of areas of responsibility, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we can see those areas in Article 1, can't we?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 1 describes the term "internal affairs." It deals with what internal affairs encompass.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the Minister of the Ministry for Internal Affairs of Macedonia is the person most responsible for the activities pertaining to internal affairs described in Article 1 of this law, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister is the person that who cares that the ministry operates and carries out its legal obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can you turn to Article 6 of the Law on Internal Affairs. The first paragraph says: "The employees of the Ministry of Internal Affairs are conducting their duties and tasks in accordance with the rights, obligations, and authorisations determined by the law and other regulations that are brought based on the law." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, below that, we see another paragraph: "An employee of the ministry must implement orders of the minister or the person authorised by him given in connection with the functions of the ministry ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "... except when implementation of the orders present a criminal offence." Now, based on Article 6, for example, the minister could give orders about operative matters, such as solving a case, can't he? Couldn't the minister tell his subordinates, "Solve the crime, find evidence, find the truth"? Couldn't the minister do that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're putting me in a position to interpret the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I can just say, Mr. Stojanovski, I'm not putting you in a position. You referred to this law during your testimony, so I'm asking you about it.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I will tell you my opinion about this Article. Article 2 -- paragraph 2 of this Article, which you're asking me about, regulates the obligation of the employee, not of the employer. Another aspect is that, according to my understanding, the minister can issue a certain order, however, within the framework of the competencies which he has. He cannot issue an order for a concrete case. Even I, from the position which I have, cannot issue an order to the unit of internal affairs how to solve a certain case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if someone came into this courtroom, like you did, and testified under oath that the minister told his subordinates, "Find the truth; work as quickly as you can," you're saying that would be a lie?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What you're saying is general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No. I'm saying something very specific. If a person came into this courtroom and said that the minister, with respect to a particular case, said, "Find the truth; work as quickly as you can; gather all the information," are you saying that would be a lie?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would not be a lie. This is not interfering in the operative matters of the units of internal affairs. This is requests for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's not --

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this request of information, it is usually done through commissions, by setting up working groups, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, although, it is not "interfering," as you say, with the operative units of the internal affairs, it would certainly have an impact on the operative units of internal affairs, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, for them to do their work in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If I can show you, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could show the witness what is tab 32. It's in the first binder provided by the Defence. It might be the last document. This is Exhibit 1D138. It's the last document in the first binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stojanovski, this is a document from the Ministry of Interior, police section, dated the 23rd of November, 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sorry. I think you've got -- yeah. I'm grateful to the usher for her able assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovski, this document is dated the 23rd of November, 2001, and it's titled: "Annex to the general plan for the return of the security forces to the towns and villages and the return of displaced persons." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says that: "This annex modifies the general plan for the return of the security forces to the towns and villages and the return of displaced residents; it extends the lists of towns and villages mentioned in part of phase three, subphase two, for the return of the security forces to these places." Then it lists a number of villages within the territory of SVR Skopje, Tetovo, Gostivar, and Kumanovo. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you see, at the bottom, this document or this annex was prepared by Risto Galevski, the head of the uniformed police; and it was approved by Goran Mitevski, the director of the public security bureau; as well as it was approved by then -- the then minister, Ljube Boskoski. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it; although, I don't see where it says "approved."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, all right. You may be correct, because you are certainly reading your native language and I am not. But it is certainly signed and stamped by Mr. Galevski, Mr. Mitevski, and Minister Boskoski. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It means that, in the least, that he was informed of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see the -- never mind. This particular plan or this operation, for lack of a better word, of sending the security forces back into a number of villages, this is not something that is specifically discussed in the Law on Internal Affairs, is it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not done from this point of view which you're just mentioning now. This is not established by the Law on Internal Affairs. I did not work. I have not had any activities related to this matter. In accordance to my understanding, this was under the auspices of the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, it is apparently also under the auspices of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, right? It was their plan to send their officers back to villages.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree. The plan was worked in accordance to the information I had, together with the OSCE and on the basis of their assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm just trying now to understand your response. Are you saying that the operation to return the security forces, Ministry of Internal Affairs forces, to villages in different parts of Macedonia and the return of displaced residents was not an operation of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, that they were somehow removed from this?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an independent operation of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Your point is, then, that this operation was carried out in association with members of the OSCE. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how accurately cooperation reflects the situation. Surely, there was cooperation, but the OSCE, as an international organisation, had a direct influence in determining the phases of this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So this was an operation of the forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, but in which members of the OSCE also had some influence. Is that a correct summary of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A decisive influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Was this operation to send the security forces back into parts of Macedonia from which they had been compelled to leave earlier, was that an illegal operation?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And wouldn't these kinds of activities also be considered as operative work of the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not operative; this is more strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, if you're moving large numbers of police officers from one place in Macedonia to another place in Macedonia after months of - to use your term - "a very complex security situation," you wouldn't call that a matter of operative work or operational work; that's only strategy?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a slightly different understanding of this. I understand the deployment or moving of forces as tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then, let me -- let me rephrase my question then. Wouldn't these kind of activities then be considered - I'll use your phrase - "tactical" work of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would consider this tactical work, strategy developed together with the OSCE and its implementation, through, what I said, the appropriate tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And anywhere that you know in the Law on Internal Affairs that authorised this particular - to use your term - "tactical" work?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The law does not specify neither operative work, nor tactical work, nor strategy work. These are usually level -- usual levels in a modern organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So, again, this would be another area of Ministry of Internal Affairs practice, which isn't specifically described or defined in the laws or regulations, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This situation was not foreseen in the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why do you suppose the minister and the director for the public security bureau signed off on this plan?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the deployment of forces -- one reason is that the deployment of forces across areas covered by many sectors for internal affairs is under the competence of the bureau for public security; on the other hand, the law prescribes that one of the duties of the minister is the international cooperation. My opinion - not necessarily the best opinion - is that one of the main reasons for the sign and the stamp belongs to this framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is that your actual knowledge, Mr. Stojanovski, or is that your speculation?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So the answer to my question was you are speculating when you have just provided this information, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
